title: Insulated systems and earth faults
where: the Electrical shelf's Supply systems folder
folderRuns: Insulated systems and earth faults, then Batteries (built alongside this one)
blurb: Why the first earth fault on an unearthed supply trips nothing, what an insulation monitor reads, and how to find the fault.
from: any Brilliant electricity or circuits course still reachable on brilliant.org, and failing that the nearest public course on earthing systems (for example a manufacturer's training course on IT systems and insulation monitoring)
others: public manufacturer guides on IT systems and insulation monitoring (Bender and similar), IEC 60364 and IEC 61557-8/-9 as titled public descriptions (no reproduced tables), marine classification society rule summaries on insulated distribution, Electrical Installation Guide (Schneider) chapters on earthing systems, and textbook chapters on marine electrical systems (contents)
syllabi: What a marine electrical engineer actually uses of this topic: the STCW Code Table A-III/6 (electro-technical officer) and A-III/1 competence lines that touch it, the MCA electro-technical officer and engineer officer syllabus lines (Electrotechnology), the public apprenticeship standards for an electrical or marine engineering technician on the Institute for Apprenticeships site, and the Pearson BTEC HN units that cover it. Exact lines. Also what Dan's BS 7671 and inspection and testing qualifications already cover of earthing systems (TN, TT and IT), so the course starts beyond them
later: Batteries (same folder, built alongside: it owns cells, charging and hydrogen)
Transformers and magnetism (it owns isolating transformers' magnetics)
scope: Insulated (IT) systems from first principles, pitched beyond Dan's BS 7671 (which is almost all TN and TT), in about this order (the brief may merge or split): (1) earthing systems compared: TN, TT and IT by what the supply's star point does, and why ships often run insulated systems (continuity after one fault); (2) the first earth fault on an insulated three-phase system: no fault current to speak of, the healthy phases rise towards line voltage to earth, the phasor picture (AC circuits built phasors: use them); (3) capacitance to earth: every cable and filter couples to earth, so 'insulated' really means earthed through capacitance, the charging current, and why a big system's first fault still passes current; (4) the second fault: two faults on different phases make a phase-to-phase fault through the hull or earth, which is why the first must be found fast; (5) watching insulation live: earth lamps and their reading, insulation monitoring devices (injection principle, alarm levels in ohms per volt as published guidance gives them), on AC and on DC systems; (6) insulated DC systems: a battery or DC switchboard with no earthed pole, the balance (bridge) method of earth detection, and what a pole-to-earth voltage tells you; (7) finding the fault: sectionalising, insulation fault location with injected test signals and clamp sensors, and insulation resistance testing of a circuit once isolated (Dan knows IR testing: build on it); (8) dangers peculiar to insulated systems: arcing (intermittent) earth faults and transient overvoltages, filters and drives giving false readings (Electronics lesson 8 named this: go deeper, not over), and safe working. Build on AC circuits (phasors, capacitance, three-phase), his BS 7671 ADS knowledge (to contrast), HV Subsea Cable Testing (fault location) and Electronics. Examples from public, general marine and industrial equipment only; never how the Royal Navy or a particular boat does it, never submarine systems beyond CLAUDE.md's public outline, and never anything from Dan's SMQ books.
